metadata.title: TMUA 2020 · Paper 2
metadata.description: Worked steps, progressive hints and reviewed follow-up questions.

matches.rationale: Both form a discriminant inequality for real quadratic intersections and keep both sign branches when solving a squared parameter bound. The candidate requires two distinct axis crossings and a region diagram; the original includes tangency when a line meets a curve.
sharedKnowledge: Both form a discriminant inequality for real quadratic intersections and keep both sign branches when solving a squared parameter bound. The candidate requires two distinct axis crossings and a region diagram; the original includes tangency when a line meets a curve.

matches.rationale: Both require an exact parameter condition for quadratic roots. Here the root separation adds an extra strict bound, so quadratic-formula work extends the original discriminant test.
Both detect tangency by substituting a line equation into a curve and requiring a repeated quadratic root. The follow-up uses the y-axis and a circle.
Both use trigonometric magnitudes together with the allowed full-turn quadrant; the follow-up obtains the magnitude from an identity rather than a tangent ratio.
Both begin from a tangent value and ask about another trigonometric quantity. This follow-up makes retaining all tangent branches and justifying the final output explicit.
Both depend on remembering that positive tangent allows quadrant III, where sine and cosine are negative. The follow-up audits the sign lost after squaring.

Both ask for the first invalid line of an algebraic argument; the crucial distinction is a sign hidden by an operation. Here the sign is lost in a principal square root rather than a subtracted bracket.

Both audit an algebraic argument line by line and locate the first unsupported equivalence, allowing that there may be no error. The original checks signs when expanding a subtraction; the candidate instead checks whether a discarded inequality bound is automatic. The shared operation is proof auditing, not the same expansion.
sharedKnowledge: Both audit an algebraic argument line by line and locate the first unsupported equivalence, allowing that there may be no error. The original checks signs when expanding a subtraction; the candidate instead checks whether a discarded inequality bound is automatic. The shared operation is proof auditing, not the same expansion.

matches.rationale: Both select non-prime integer counterexamples only after checking the exact domain or residue condition. Here all qualifying failures below 50 must be counted.
Both distinguish a composite number that refutes a prime claim from one outside the premise or supporting the conclusion.
Both offer three potential integer counterexamples, one of which is disqualified by the hypothesis despite appearing relevant.
Both identify exponential graphs from landmark values and behaviour, without requiring differentiation. This follow-up compares base and input scaling rather than a quotient’s asymptotes.
Both choose a sketch from positivity, end behaviour and an exact interior point. This follow-up uses a variable-base logarithm instead of a bounded exponential quotient.
Both distinguish graphs by limiting behaviour and one convenient exact value. This follow-up has trigonometric bases and exponents and requires keeping open endpoints distinct from evaluations.
Both test a logical condition for signed-integral cancellation. The follow-up asks for sufficiency and cancellation around the midpoint 2, making the implication direction explicit.
Both ask whether a stated structural condition is necessary or sufficient for a zero or equal signed integral. The follow-up checks both directions for complete sine periods.
sharedKnowledge: Both ask whether a stated structural condition is necessary or sufficient for a zero or equal signed integral. The follow-up checks both directions for complete sine periods.

matches.rationale: Both use a function satisfying a whole-interval condition to test an integral claim. Odd cancellation and a nonnegative square distinguish total behaviour from pointwise restrictions.
sharedKnowledge: Both use a function satisfying a whole-interval condition to test an integral claim. Odd cancellation and a nonnegative square distinguish total behaviour from pointwise restrictions.

matches.rationale: Both test whether perpendicular diagonals force stronger symmetry or square properties. Explicit non-square quadrilaterals show why the extra property need not follow.
Both classify geometric conditions by necessity or sufficiency, keeping the exact named side pairs and quadrilateral target fixed.
Both disprove an algebraic statement asserted for all allowed pairs by evaluating a single admissible pair and checking whether the two sides agree.
sharedKnowledge: Both disprove an algebraic statement asserted for all allowed pairs by evaluating a single admissible pair and checking whether the two sides agree.

matches.rationale: Both add simultaneous inequalities to prove one universal conclusion and use feasible counterexamples to reject tempting additional conclusions.
Both test claimed deductions from simultaneous inequalities and require counterexamples satisfying both original assumptions. The follow-up highlights unsafe subtraction or multiplication.
Both decide which inequalities must hold under all stated order restrictions. This follow-up concentrates on reversing order under negative multiplication and division.
Both encode a drawn path as a sequence of constrained movements and check where the path may lie. The follow-up tests valid path transformations rather than another expanding spiral.
The same chord-versus-curve reasoning connects a universal midpoint inequality to the sign of the second derivative; necessity must be distinguished from sufficiency.
Both reason about the direction of trapezium error without evaluating the integrals. This version tracks error under reflection and complementary function heights.
Directly applies the upward/downward bending criterion for trapezium over- and underestimates after graph transformations.
The integral-order claim uses a pointwise nonnegative difference, closely matching the original use of a nonnegative square. Other claims test the separate roles of function and derivative.
sharedKnowledge: The integral-order claim uses a pointwise nonnegative difference, closely matching the original use of a nonnegative square. Other claims test the separate roles of function and derivative.

matches.rationale: Both infer necessary statements from an integral identity or sign, using the actual integration interval and rejecting unsupported pointwise conclusions.
sharedKnowledge: Both infer necessary statements from an integral identity or sign, using the actual integration interval and rejecting unsupported pointwise conclusions.

matches.rationale: Both impose an arithmetic-series sum condition on integer parameters and test purported parity necessities with fully allowed counterexamples.
Both translate relations between AP partial sums into a condition on a and d, then avoid overclaiming separate parameter signs.
Both require parity and integer-domain restrictions to survive an AP formula rather than treating a real algebraic expression as automatically an allowed integer.
A trigonometric sum is evaluated by proving a repeating block has zero sum and retaining the final partial block.
A parity-dependent recurrence gives a short periodic block whose sum replaces inappropriate AP/GP formulae.
Both determine distant behaviour from a proved cycle and index remainder; the follow-up adds a non-repeating initial segment.
Both audit a displayed calculation and identify the first unsupported step by checking the exact condition of the rule used. The follow-up concerns cancellation rather than FTC.
Both require identifying what is variable in a definite integral before applying a familiar calculus rule. Here the previous sequence term is constant; there is no moving-endpoint derivative.
Both order data, convert a mean to a total, combine median and range constraints, and prove an extremal value with an attaining list. Repetitions are permitted in this follow-up.
Targets the same danger of choosing separate extrema that cannot coexist in one permitted configuration. It asks which extrema bounds are valid rather than optimising a median or range.
Uses continuity and opposite-sign tails of a genuine cubic to force a real zero, which is precisely why the original difference cannot retain a cubic term while staying positive.
sharedKnowledge: Uses continuity and opposite-sign tails of a genuine cubic to force a real zero, which is precisely why the original difference cannot retain a cubic term while staying positive.

matches.rationale: Analyses cubic end behaviour and turning heights under a parameter, with careful boundaries and sufficient versus complete conditions.

Both assign truth values to all interdependent statements in one shared configuration, split exhaustive cases and reject any assignment inconsistent with its own truth count. The grid task additionally negates neighbour quantifiers and uses geometric symmetry; the other question uses a common urn count or an unknown factual atom and speaker-count assertions. The shared operation is whole-configuration truth consistency.

The shared operation is whole-configuration truth consistency.

matches.rationale: Both translate a local neighbour requirement into coverage and justify attainable extremal arrangements. The seating question isolates circular coverage by occupied neighbours; the grid question first derives coverage by truthful neighbours, adds the prohibition on adjacent truthful cells and also asks for a maximum. This is a coverage prerequisite transfer, not the same full truth puzzle.

matches.rationale: Both use an exactly-one-true premise to exclude any option that forces another true option. The candidate uses iff-to-if implications and nested input sets; the original additionally uses contrapositives of strict sign rules.
sharedKnowledge: Both use an exactly-one-true premise to exclude any option that forces another true option. The candidate uses iff-to-if implications and nested input sets; the original additionally uses contrapositives of strict sign rules.

matches.rationale: Both translate only-if and sufficient-condition wording and distinguish equivalent contrapositives from converse or inverse claims. The candidate compares three forms with a given prime theorem instead of enforcing one sole true function rule.
sharedKnowledge: Both translate only-if and sufficient-condition wording and distinguish equivalent contrapositives from converse or inverse claims. The candidate compares three forms with a given prime theorem instead of enforcing one sole true function rule.

matches.rationale: Direct prerequisite: convert the numerical measure of the same angle. This checks the reverse conversion direction to the original and explicitly reinforces that a scalar multiplier outside sine is unaffected.
Transfer to a degree-based input 2x: keep the input angle and its interval separate from x. The extra simultaneous-equation work is explicit; this is not another calculator-mode question.

Both require checking an attempted proof in order and identifying its first unsupported line. The original failure is algebraic sign handling; this follow-up tests unjustified factor matching, so it transfers the proof-audit discipline rather than repeating the same algebra error.
sharedKnowledge: true conclusion does not validate a proof

matches.rationale: Both use one allowed counterexample to refute a universal claim. The follow-up adds a prime-number premise, making the student check that a proposed counterexample actually satisfies the hypothesis.

Both infer signed-integral comparisons from nonnegative differences on common forward intervals, without requiring antiderivatives. The candidate practises this order-preservation step by comparing three exponential integrands; it adds exponent ordering and does not reproduce the original square-integral identity or somewhere sign conclusion.
sharedKnowledge: Both infer signed-integral comparisons from nonnegative differences on common forward intervals, without requiring antiderivatives. The candidate practises this order-preservation step by comparing three exponential integrands; it adds exponent ordering and does not reproduce the original square-integral identity or somewhere sign conclusion.

matches.rationale: Both begin with the definition of a median in sorted data. The original requires distinct triples and a least-range construction; this simpler follow-up deliberately permits repetition and tests necessary versus sufficient conditions. It reinforces median and hypothesis handling, not the original extremal argument.

Both compare implications between whole statements and use an exact-count requirement. The original eliminates options forcing another truth; the candidate explicitly counts which condition guarantees exactly three other conditions by containment of their real solution sets.
sharedKnowledge: Both compare implications between whole statements and use an exact-count requirement. The original eliminates options forcing another truth; the candidate explicitly counts which condition guarantees exactly three other conditions by containment of their real solution sets.

matches.rationale: Both demand executing every part of a differentiation operation rather than dropping a factor. This recurrence uses the power rule followed by multiplication by x and adds a geometric sum; it does not practise the original fundamental-theorem and chain-rule upper-limit calculation directly.
sharedKnowledge: retain all factors in the stated operation

matches.rationale: Both use leading-term behaviour at the two ends of the real line to rule out a proposed polynomial property. The original forces a cubic difference to lose its odd-degree leading term; this follow-up combines quintic tail behaviour with derivative sign changes and extrema counts.
